newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: SOCCER-AJAX TRADE YOUTH FOR EXPERIENCE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-AJAX TRADE YOUTH FOR EXPERIENCE.

text.p: Ajax Amsterdam, the Netherland's flagship club, have long enjoyed a reputation for developing home-grown young talent.

However, the traditionalists, who have already come to terms with the departure of highly-successful coach Louis van Gaal and a host of top players at the end of last season, could be in for a shock next month.
When Ajax kick off the new season in August, supporters will be cheering on a rather older team with a Danish coach and more foreigners than ever before.

Supporters in southern Europe and England have become accustomed to cosmopolitan sides, but Ajax's signings mark a departure for a club whose considerable success has been built on a tried and tested youth policy.

A smattering of outside talent has already appeared in Ajax's red and white -- Nigerian Tijani Babangida and Finn Jari Litmanen were regular starters last season -- but the net has now been spread far more widely.
Of the 10 close season signings, only three are Dutch nationals. The arrivals include two Danes, a Costa Rican, a Georgian, a Nigerian, a Pole and a South African.
The foreign complement could rise further if, as expected, Brazilian defender Marcio Santos, on loan to Atletico Mineiro, returns to Amsterdam.
The signings are required to plug the gaps following the departure of home products.

Patrick Kluivert, Winston Bogarde, Marc Overmars and Arnold Scholten have all left for foreign sides, following on the heels of Clarence Seedorf, Michael Reiziger and Edgar Davids who departed a year ago.
Dutch international Overmars, whose skills helped Ajax win the European Cup in 1995, has joined Arsenal.
Kluivert and Bogarde have gone to AC Milan, while veteran midfielder Scholten has moved to Japan.
Ajax acknowledges it has responded too slowly to the changes brought about by the Bosman ruling which allows players out of contract freely to leave their clubs.
"We couldn't make up for their loss from our youth, so we have had to bring in many players," club treasurer Arie van Os said recently.
"Now everyone is in for the long-term and we can build for the future."
The changes trade youth for experience. Ajax's biggest name signing, Michael Laudrup, is 33.
Coach Morten Olsen, the former Danish international captain who was a surprise choice to take over at the club, said the newcomers still had to prove themselves.
"The most important thing is that the new foreign players identify themselves with Ajax," he said.
He urged them to fight for Ajax, to fight for their places and said he was starting with a blank slate
"There are no certain starters in my side."
Competition will be fiercer as Olsen will pick his sides from an enlarged 25-man squad. Previous coach van Gaal operated with a squad of about 18.
Dutch media, so far, seem content that the new man has pinned his colours firmly to the Ajax mast and already has a reasonable mastery of the language.

Olsen is known as a perfectionist whose managerial career has been less impressive than his playing years. He coached Brondby in Denmark before moving to Cologne in Germany, where he was sacked after four seasons.
"Morten Olsen presents himself in style," declared top-selling newspaper De Telegraaf last weekend.
Financially, Ajax is in also good shape. Its new stadium and progress to the European Cup semifinals last season guaranteed the club healthy receipts.
Last season, Ajax also registered a record income of 80 million guilders ($39.5 million).
This season, treasurer Van Os believes the income will reach 70 million guilders with an expected 44,000 season-ticket holders.
As for the future, Olsen said neither he nor the board had set firm goals, but he will not want a repeat of last season when poor early form left the club only able to climb to fourth by the end.
"Ajax must always go for the title, but you need luck actually to win something.... What is important is the way we play. We are here to entertain," he said.
